quotes.t: It is not that I am mad, it is only that my head is different from yours.
quotes.c: Quoted by Stobaeus, Stobaeus, iii. 3. 51

quotes.t: Poverty is a virtue which one can teach oneself.
quotes.c: Quoted by Stobaeus, Stobaeus, iv. 32a. 19

quotes.t: Aristotle dines when it seems good to King Philip, but Diogenes when he himself pleases.
quotes.c: Quoted by Plutarch, Plutarch, On Exile, 12 (Moralia, 604D)

quotes.t: Asked where he came from, he said, "I am a citizen of the world."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 63

quotes.t: Being asked where in Greece he saw good men, he replied, "Good men nowhere, but good boys at Sparta."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 27

quotes.t: Boasting, like gilded armour, is very different inside from outside.
quotes.c: Quoted by Stobaeus, Stobaeus, iii. 22. 40

quotes.t: Diogenes the cynic, seeing one of the so-called freedmen pluming himself, while many heartily congratulated him, marveled at the absence of reason and discernment. "A man might as well," he said, "proclaim that one of his servants became a grammarian, a geometrician, or musician, when he has no idea whatever of the art." For as the proclamation cannot make them men of knowledge, so neither can it make them free.
quotes.c: Quoted by Philo, Philo, Every Good Man is Free, F. H. Colson, trans. (1941), 157

quotes.t: He lit a lamp in broad daylight and said, as he went about, "I am looking for a human."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 41. This line is frequently translated as "I am looking for an honest man."

quotes.t: He once begged alms of a statue, and, when asked why he did so, replied, "To get practice in being refused."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 49

quotes.t: He used to reason as follows: 'Everything belongs to the gods; the wise are friends of the gods; friends hold all things in common; ergo, everything belongs to the wise.'
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 37, as reported in Diogenes the Cynic: Sayings and Anecdotes as translated by Robin Hard (Oxford: 2012), p. 13

quotes.t: He was breakfasting in the marketplace, and the bystanders gathered round him with cries of "dog." "It is you who are dogs," cried he, "when you stand round and watch me at my breakfast."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 61

quotes.t: He was going into a theatre, meeting face to face those who were coming out, and being asked why, "This," he said, "is what I practise doing all my life."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 64

quotes.t: He was seized and dragged off to King Philip, and being asked who he was, replied, "A spy upon your insatiable greed."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 43. Cf. Plutarch, Moralia, 70CD.

quotes.t: If you are to be kept right, you must possess either good friends or red-hot enemies. The one will warn you, the other will expose you.
quotes.c: Quoted by Plutarch, Plutarch, Moralia, 74C

quotes.t: On reaching Athens he fell in with Antisthenes. Being repulsed by him, because he never welcomed pupils, by sheer persistence Diogenes wore him out. Once when he stretched out his staff against him, the pupil offered his head with the words, "Strike, for you will find no wood hard enough to keep me away from you, so long as I think you've something to say."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 21

quotes.t: Once he saw the officials of a temple leading away some one who had stolen a bowl belonging to the treasurers, and said, "The great thieves are leading away the little thief."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 45

quotes.t: One day, observing a child drinking out of his hands, he cast away the cup from his wallet with the words, "A child has beaten me in plainness of living."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 37

quotes.t: Perdiccas threatened to put him to death unless he came to him, "That's nothing wonderful," Diogenes said, "for a beetle or a tarantula would do the same."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 44

quotes.t: Plato had defined Man as an animal, biped and featherless, and was applauded. Diogenes plucked a fowl and brought it into the lecture-room with the words, "Behold Plato's man!"
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 40

quotes.t: Self-taught poverty is a help toward philosophy, for the things which philosophy attempts to teach by reasoning, poverty forces us to practice.
quotes.c: Quoted by Stobaeus, Stobaeus, iv. 32a. 11

quotes.t: The noblest people are those despising wealth, learning, pleasure and life; esteeming above them poverty, ignorance, hardship and death.
quotes.c: Quoted by Stobaeus, Stobaeus, iv. 29a. 19

quotes.t: Thieves and fighters do not come from eaters of barley-bread; but informers and tyrants come from meat-eaters.
quotes.c: Quoted by Porphyry, Porphyry, On Abstinence from Killing Animals as translated by Gillian Clark (2000), 1, 47, 3

quotes.t: To Xeniades, who had purchased Diogenes at the slave market, he said, "Come, see that you obey orders."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 36

quotes.t: To one who asked what was the proper time for lunch, he said, "If a rich man, when you will; if a poor man, when you can."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 40

quotes.t: To the question what wine he found pleasant to drink, he replied, "That for which other people pay."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 54

quotes.t: Virtue cannot dwell with wealth either in a city or in a house.
quotes.c: Quoted by Stobaeus, Stobaeus, iv. 31c. 88

quotes.t: When Alexander the Great addressed him with greetings, and asked if he wanted anything, Diogenes replied "Yes, stand a little out of my sunshine."
quotes.c: Quoted by Plutarch, From Plutarch, Alexander, 14. Cf. Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 38, Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, v. 32

quotes.t: When asked why people give to beggars but not to philosophers, he replied, 'Because they expect they may become lame and blind, but never that they will become philosophers.'
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 56, as reported in Diogenes the Cynic: Sayings and Anecdotes as translated by Robin Hard (Oxford: 2012), p. 18

quotes.t: When people laughed at him because he walked backward beneath the portico, he said to them: "Aren't you ashamed, you who walk backward along the whole path of existence, and blame me for walking backward along the path of the promenade?"
quotes.c: Quoted by Stobaeus, Stobaeus, iii. 4. 83

quotes.t: When scolded for masturbating in public, he said "I wish it were as easy to banish hunger by rubbing my belly."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 46, 69 Variant: If only it were as easy to banish hunger by rubbing the belly as it is to masturbate. As quoted in Encarta Book of Quotations (2000) edited by Bill Swainson, p. 274

quotes.t: When some one boasted that at the Pythian games he had vanquished men, Diogenes replied, "Nay, I defeat men, you defeat slaves."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 33, 43

quotes.t: When some one reminded him that the people of Sinope had sentenced him to exile, he said, "And I sentenced them to stay at home."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 49

quotes.t: When the slave auctioneer asked in what he was proficient, he replied, "In ruling people."
quotes.c: Quoted by Diogenes Laërtius, Diogenes Laërtius, vi. 74

quotes.t: οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι κύνες τοὺς ἐχθροὺς δάκνουσιν, ἐγὼ δὲ τοὺς φίλους, ἵνα σώσω.
quotes.c: Quoted by Stobaeus, Other dogs bite only their enemies, whereas I bite also my friends in order to save them. Stobaeus, iii. 13. 44

quotes.t: Wise kings generally have wise counselors; and he must be a wise man himself who is capable of distinguishing one.
Dogs and philosophers do the greatest good and get the fewest rewards.
I am a citizen of the world, and my country is the world.
I am not an Athenian or a Greek, but a citizen of the world.
It is the privilege of the gods to want nothing, and of godlike men to want little.
Man is the most intelligent of the animals - and the most silly.
The foundation of every state is the education of its youth.
Those who have virtue always in their mouths, and neglect it in practice, are like a harp, which emits a sound pleasing to others, while itself is insensible of the music.
When I look upon seamen, men of science and philosophers, man is the wisest of all beings; when I look upon priests and prophets nothing is as contemptible as man.
He who does not need anything is the richest man.
I am a dog, and I bark at falsehood.
I am a lamp that is always lit.
I am a man who has nothing, and I am at peace.
I am a man who has nothing, and I am content.
I am a man who wants nothing, and everything.
I have nothing to ask but that you would remove to the other side, that I may enjoy the sun.
If you want to make a man happy, do not add to his riches but take away from his desires.
The art of being free is the art of living.
The foundation of every state is good education.
Wise leaders generally have wise counselors because it takes a wise person themselves to distinguish them.
